Subject: TTFT & streaming SLO follow-up (post-call recap)

Thanks for the call earlier — great overview of your streaming UX and throughput goals. Quick recap + next steps so we have alignment before the technical runbook: 

Summary / goals
- Target TTFT (time-to-first-token): 200ms p50 and <= 500ms p99 under expected steady-state load.
- Streaming: client requires chunked streaming for progressive rendering (SSE preferred, WebSocket acceptable). Chunk cadence target: ~50-100ms between flushes for smooth UI.
- Throughput: 500 concurrent QPS expected initially; plan for burst to 1,000 QPS during peak.
- Concurrency/capacity: multiple concurrent users with average 3 simultaneous streaming sessions per user.

Risks & constraints we noted
- Cold-starts impacting TTFT for infrequent endpoints — need warm pool or fast cold path.
- Batching helps throughput but can increase TTFT for first token; likely need a low-latency path with batching disabled.
- Network latency (client-side) will add to TTFT — network topology doc requested.

Attachments (sent separately): SLO spreadsheet (format we use for perf acceptance) and a network/topology stub.

Immediate next steps
1) I'll send the SLO template and our suggested measurement setup (attached).
2) Aditya to scope a perf test on our staging cluster using a sample payload you provide (propose Wed 7/14).
3) Alex/Bethany to confirm whether SSE or WebSocket is preferred and share a sample client payload and expected average token length.
4) We'll propose an initial canary configuration: low-latency endpoint (no batching, quantized fast model) + standard endpoint for bulk traffic.

If that matches your notes, we can lock in the technical call with Aditya to run the first perf sweep.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
Enterprise AE | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — very helpful. A couple of clarifying questions before we lock the test window:

1) SSE vs WebSocket: our frontend team prefers WebSocket for bidirectional events, but SSE is easier to integrate with our current server-side infra. Does Redwood provide both with comparable latency characteristics? Any preference for hitting the TTFT target?

2) Chunk cadence: you mentioned 50-100ms. Is that measured from server-side flush to client-render-ready, or is there any additional recommended padding for transport? Our client will reassemble chunks so minimal padding is preferred.

3) p99 under load: how do you measure TTFT p99 in a way that separates network tail from server side? We want the server-side guaranteed p99 <= 500ms if possible (we can control client-side network).

4) Sample payload: attaching an example JSON (small chatbot prompt, avg 120 tokens). Looking to confirm expected tokenization behavior / chunk sizes.

If Wednesday (7/14) works for your team, we can run the perf test in the afternoon after our engineering sync.

—Alex

Great questions — answered inline below plus attached the SLO template and a network/topology diagram for your infra team.

1) SSE vs WebSocket: Redwood supports both. In our experience, raw server-side flush cadence and the serving runtime's immediate write behavior matter more than protocol. WebSocket can be slightly better for bidirectional patterns; SSE is simpler for uni-directional streaming. For strict TTFT targets we recommend keeping a dedicated low-latency endpoint (no batching, minimal pre-processing) regardless of protocol.

2) Chunk cadence: our 50-100ms guidance is server flush cadence (server-side inter-chunk interval). Expect an additional 10-30ms on average for transport within the same region; cross-region adds more. We'll log server-side timestamps so we can separate transport tail from server processing in the perf results.

3) p99 measurement: we'll run server-side instrumentation that records time-to-first-byte and time-to-first-token at the server boundary (after the model emits first token). That gives a server-only p99. We'll share the measurement script along with the SLO template.

4) Sample payload: got it — thanks. For the test we'll use your sample plus a few synthetic variations (short/long prompts) to ensure behavior across token lengths.

Proposed test cadence (Wed 7/14)
- 13:00 PT: quick sync (15 min) to confirm payloads and endpoints
- 13:15 PT: run baseline tests (single-instance low-latency path)
- 13:45 PT: ramp to target throughput (500 QPS) and capture p50/p95/p99
- 14:30 PT: review results and adjust config (batching/quantization/cold pool)

Attached: slo_requirements.xlsx, network-topology.png

Subject: Internal: perf test plan + quick notes re: TTFT approach

Internal notes for the test (not sent to Acme yet):
- To hit ~200ms TTFT p50 and <=500ms p99 server-side we should: 
  * Use a low-latency model variant (FP16 quantized where it preserves logits timing) and disable CPU pre/post-processing where possible.
  * Provision a warm pool (min-instances) for the low-latency endpoint to avoid cold-start jitter.
  * Disable request-level batching on the low-latency path; keep batching enabled on standard endpoints.
  * Ensure the runtime flushes tokens as they are generated — set streaming flush cadence to ~80ms (compromise between throughput and client rendering smoothness).
  * Keep SSE and WebSocket implementation parity: both will use identical server flush logic.

- Test plan: run baseline perf (single instance), then horizontal scale (up to 8 instances) while ramping to 500 QPS. Capture server-side time-to-first-byte and time-to-first-token with our instrumentation.

- Measurement: we'll separate server-side TTFT (at model emit) and network transport (using tcpdump/trace at load generator) to produce corrected server p99.

I'll own the orchestration + perf harness; Dev — can you validate that the staging cluster has the low-latency variant and the warm pool configured? I'll provision test keys and share the DocuSign PO link once we confirm the window.

Thanks,
Aditya
Principal SWE, Serving & Runtime | Redwood Inference
